title: The Zone of Interest…or how Jonathan Frazer examines the capability of seemingly ordinary people to do monstrous things, and appearance and first impressions and trustworthiness vs reality/gut feeling.

commenti.body: I'd push back a little bit on your idea that the Höss family is "ordinary." I don't think Zone of Interest is a comment on how ordinary people can commit monstrous acts, but rather a comment on how people compartmentalize these things when they are otherwise benefiting from them.

Yes, but at the same time Rudolf WAS committing these acts, however indirectly, of evil. People are capable of compartmentalizing things whilst committing these acts that they see as benefiting themselves, and that happens all the time with people like serial killers for example. And those who are complicit and willing to allow those acts to be committed are just as much active perpetrators and indirectly committing these acts as much as those do directly. 

And I am saying that in the world of the film, the Hoss family would seem ordinary, at least to people who weren’t in the camps that Rudolf commanded. I mean, think about it. People who weren’t in Auschwitz or any of the camps would have looked at the Hoss family would not have seen the sociopathic tendencies of the couple or of Rudolf. People who were visitors at that house or who interacted with them in day to day life without knowing or paying attention to what was going on the outside of the home wouldn’t have thought that they were monsters, instead seeing a beautiful ordinary happy family living the life that all of them wanted, and a lot of people would have envied the life they had, ignoring the whole Auschwitz bit. I mean, ignoring the whole Auschwitz situation, who wouldn’t have been jealous of the family? They seemingly had everything: gorgeous house, a high paying secure job with lots of quirks (nevermind that that job actively involved committing crimes against humanity on a daily basis), servants, beautiful kids, gorgeous wife, adorable baby…and a pool with a slide! I mean, if I were to have a house like that that wasn’t beside a concentration camp, I would love to have something like that. 

And again: Rudolf, if we were to ignore his job and his apathy to the acts that he is committing, doesn’t seem or look like a monster on the outside. He’s handsome, intelligent, soft spoken and a hard worker who’s also a devoted family man who wants nothing but the best for his kids. A similar thing could be said about Hedwig, minus the hard worker bit. Most people who would meet someone like them in day to day life without knowing about what Rudolf does for a living would assume that the couple would be good people, since many of the personality characteristics would normally be seen as positive by people on the outside. That trustworthy unassuming aspect to their personalities allows them to be complicit in the apathy of them committing these acts (whether indirectly through participating in complicity like Hedwig with the belongings of the concentration camp inmates or directly participating through the day to day work for their job like Rudolf), and therefore indirectly perpetrating these acts of monstrosity. 

Many people in day to day life who think of themselves as normal upstanding citizens can be just as indirectly capable of committing acts of monstrosity as those who commit them are, and 

Again, to those people who weren’t in the camps or who interacted with Rudolf and his family in the outside world or otherwise would not think of them as being monsters.

I mean, Hedwig certainly interacts with (and tyrannizes) all of the workers in the house. Like the above poster said, I think the film is moreso abut compartementalization, and precisely how about all the great things and the great life they have depend on pretty direct murder and exploitation.

I don't even think the film is about how they are sociopathic monsters or whatever, and it never even delves into their psychology, which is why it's so interesting: it's about how and for which very material reasons they are able to not ignore but be indifferent to something that traumatizes even convincent nazis like Hedwig's mother.

I agree with the second paragraph but I would push back on the idea that it's about compartmentalization. I mean, the only moment the father seems happy is when it's announced that he's to go back to Auschwitz, and less so for being reunited with his family than the "work" that he'll continue to oversee again. Likewise Hedwig casually threatens one of the maids that she can have her husband burn her up (or something to that effect). The Hösses are so indifferent to the slaughter of Jews - to them it is the natural, corrective course of things - that I don't think they even need to rationalize and compartmentalize. (Which is why the retching scene - /premonition of the future - rings hollow/false imo; with the way that Glazer depicts him, it's almost comical to imagine a conscience within Rudolf.)

Yeah I think the part with the apple girl shows some ordinary people gave a shit. Even her mom who is obviously just as materialistic and shallow as the daughter, and doesn't like Jewish people, still felt sick and had to leave.

They're not supposed to be ordinary  people who remind us we are all capable of evil, or who are hiding their monstrous side, they are just evil. Evil itself is ordinary.

There is just no need to have any complex motivations or personality to be able to be evil, it is a result of stupid and average traits. I don't think the movie glamorized either of them, neither of them has any impressive qualities. She's just materialistic and obsessed with her house and things she gets to take from the Jews, he is like some middle management type bureaucrat who feels so proud to get any praise from his superiors. They're not exceptionally smart, they're boring, all their preoccupations are mundane as fuck, there's no depth to them (in a realistic way, it didn't feel like a caricature), and they're also evil. Not despite that, but because of that. As in, evil is not that deep.

I thought the movie was almost the opposite of what you're saying, the "zone of interest" to me was the complication of sympthazing with them as humans, and genuinely being lulled into understanding their point of view, not in the sense of justifying it, but understanding the path they followed to get there. For me the discomfort and ambivalence comes from actually liking the family, and \*not\* feeling a pull to demonize them necessarily. It's like I feel I \*should\* loathe them, but my gut feelings lean more towards pity. Which is super confusing.   
  
Not "banality of evil" exactly, but ubiquity of humanity? Idk, something like that
